rv.q: And, oh, the pleasure of their company.
Not to mention the funniest show in town.
The smart, 95-minute two-hander created by and starring comedians Nick Kroll and John Mulaney dares to be hilarious, without a nanosecond of deeper meaning.
Their brand of comedy is a winning melange of all the brows: low, middle and high.
It is also uproariously, stomach-achingly funny.
It’s hard not to laugh at the running motif of their affected mispronunciation of ordinary words, like dialorg and Broadway, with a strong emphasis on the second syllable.
“Oh, Hello on Broadway” might not be the show to win over new enthusiasts.
They make mustiness new, and they're a New York City must.

The show, iterations of which have been enthusiastically embraced on the road and Off-Broadway, bungees around with absurd, occasional cleverness, with dated references to Blue Man Group and softball observations about theater cliches.
But it starts out funny and moves past hysterical to sublime.

You're there to see Kroll and Mulaney's masterful take on the Faizon and St. Geegland — two incredibly nuanced and well-rounded characters who manage to be wildly offensive and incredibly loveable at the same time.

Far from being a sketch that wears out its welcome after the first 10 minutes, Oh, Hello turns out to be a bottomless well of funny refilled by the tragic circumstance of Gil and George being life partners by default (much like Felix and Oscar, Bert and Ernie, and Vladimir and Estragon).
The Oh, Hello devoted left the Lyceum in audible bliss, while newcomers were happily dazed by the onslaught of jokes, skits, wordplay, meta-everything, and verbal carnage.
That's theatre magic and, like it or not, Oh, Hello on Broadway is packed with it.
As staged by Alex Timbers (the freethinking director behind “Peter and the Starcatcher” and “Bloody Bloody Andrew Jackson”), “Oh, Hello” is 95 minutes of politically incorrect, gleefully silly fun.
Deftly shuffling elements of recognition and surprise, Kroll and Mulaney keep the audience in giddy laughter.

It's a sketch, drawn out. What's actually most interesting, if not really explored, is Kroll and Mulaney's obvious love for theater, through their jokes about recurring dramatic devices - the one-sided phone call, the bloody handkerchief that indicates imminent death, the profound curtain line - and bits of shtick about other plays.
After seeing Oh, Hello on Broadway , even this grumpy old reviewer found them pretty funny.

The ninety-minute evening allows for bits of improvisational riffing and Kroll and Mulaney have perfected a loose chemistry that plays on a low-key level, so jokes about dark subjects like 9/11, O.J. Simpson and JonBenet Ramsey pop out unexpectedly.
There are moments that had me in stitches, but the show’s so shapeless and shaggy that it doesn’t add up to much.
But, over 95 minutes, there is also a fair share of clunkers, bottom-drawer lines such as a reference to "Tennessee Williams and his sister Serena."
For those just meeting them, it’s an awfully long first date.
Much of Oh Hello on Broadway struck me as inside jokes that everybody in the audience seemed to get except me: “You know when you’re walking by a travel agency and you’re like….what?!”
In the final analysis, Oh, Hello and its two malapropism-prone stars will attract fans who love this kind of wise-ass humor, but, for me, the nasty tone outweighs their cleverness.
The big problem with “Oh, Hello on Broadway,” which opened Monday at the Lyceum Theatre in New York, is that Mulaney doesn’t deliver.
Expect non-stop laughs, and I mean non-stop.
For an audience of theatre and comedy nerds, Kroll and Mulaney’s (or is it Faizon and St. Geegland’s) love letter, perhaps stalker note they say, to the theatre is simply hilarious.
It was worth every drop of blue ink that I aquired.
Filled with jokes and bits that are often politically incorrect and also occasionally unprintable, "Oh, Hello on Broadway" is a supremely enjoyable and satisfying experience.
It observes and skewers pop culture – and whatever else it can get its hands on – with laser-like precision and sets up jokes with skill and care.

Mature theatergoers who are already fans of the shtick should leave the Lyceum Theater thoroughly satisfied and those who just met these cantankerous upper west siders will be, as Gil says, “Charmed, I’m sure.”
I know I'm way out of the mainstream on this one, so I must leave it to you.
What you get is 100 minutes of stupidity.
Whether one “gets” the show’s humor or not, one cannot ignore the fact that Mr. Kroll and Mr. Delaney have a marvelous chemistry together as a comedy team.

cn.t: Critics are mostly charmed by Kroll and Mulaney's crotchety Upper West Side alter egos, praising their sharp comic chemistry. Some find the cult sketch stretched thin for Broadway, but fans of the duo will howl.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
